meta.title: The Praise Setup
meta.subtitle: 12 Cards for Reading the Move Inside the Compliment
meta.description: Praise is one of the cleanest moves in the social toolkit. It costs nothing to give and costs you everything if you miss it. This dossier teaches you to read the setup before the ask lands, answer each on its own terms, and name the pattern out loud when it runs one too many times.
meta.author: AI

generation.topic: Detecting when praise is really a setup

cards.title: Praise With No Trigger Is the First Tell
cards.hook: Real praise follows something you did. Praise that arrives out of nowhere is not about you — it is about what is coming next.
cards.truth:
Setup praise does not need a reason because the reason is the ask, not your performance.
• Unprompted praise lowers your guard before the request lands.
• You feel good, which makes saying no feel like ingratitude.
• The ask always follows — within minutes or within days.
cards.remember: When praise has no trigger, a request is already on the way.
cards.theySee: A manager stopping by your desk with a wide smile before you have done anything different this week.

signals.t: They praised you but you cannot point to anything you did in the last week that earned it.
They are cheerful and warm but there is no specific event on the table yet.
They compliment you, then go quiet and wait — the gap is deliberate.
They watch your expression closely right after the compliment, checking how it landed.

steps.title: List what you did recently
steps.desc: Write the last three things you did at work or home. If none of them could explain this praise, flag the conversation.

steps.title: Hold the silence
steps.desc: After they praise you, say nothing. Count to five. The ask will surface on its own.

steps.title: Ask the open question
steps.desc: Say 'What is going on?' before you agree to anything. Get the request in plain sight first.

cards.script: "That is nice to hear — what is on your mind?"
cards.counter:
When someone praises you to move you, your job is to get the ask on the table before you respond to either.
• Notice: praise that arrives before a meeting, a favor, or a big conversation.
• Say: 'I appreciate it — what did you need?' Make them name it.
• Do: hold your answer to the ask until you have heard it fully.
cards.insight: Most people react to the praise and skip right past the ask. The ask is the only thing that matters. The harder problem is that even when you see the setup coming, the dopamine still lands — and the next card explains exactly why.
cards.scenario: Your manager finds you in the hallway and says 'I just want you to know you are one of the best people on this team' — with nothing specific and nothing on the calendar that would explain it.

cards.title: Your Brain Treats Praise Like Cash
cards.hook: When someone praises you, your brain releases dopamine. You feel better. Your threat-detection goes quiet. The person praising you just bought easier access — for free.
cards.truth:
Praise hijacks your brain's reward system before your judgment catches up.
• Dopamine fires on praise the same way it fires on money or a good meal.
• Your threat-detection quiets — you feel safer than you actually are.
• The window right after praise is when a request hits you the hardest.
cards.remember: Praise makes your brain feel paid before you have agreed to anything.
cards.theySee: A person nodding slowly, smiling, visibly relaxing their posture after being told they did great.

signals.t: You notice a physical ease or quiet pleasure settling in right after the compliment.
You find yourself saying yes before you have thought through what you are agreeing to.
Refusing in this moment feels rude or ungrateful, not just inconvenient.
You stop asking follow-up questions about what you are actually committing to.

steps.title: Name the feeling out loud inside your head
steps.desc: When the warmth hits, say to yourself: 'I just got a dopamine hit.' Naming it slows it down.

steps.title: Add ten seconds before you respond
steps.desc: Do not fill the air. Wait ten seconds after praise lands. The warmth starts to level off on its own.

steps.title: Read the ask cold
steps.desc: Repeat the request to yourself as if someone you barely like asked it. Does it still sound reasonable?

cards.script: "Let me think about that for a second."
cards.counter:
If someone praises you right before asking for something, the timing was deliberate.
• Notice: the warmth, the ease, a sudden urge to say yes before they have finished talking.
• Say: nothing yet — wait for the full request before you speak.
• Do: evaluate the ask the same way you would if no praise had been given.
cards.insight: The dopamine hit from praise and the dopamine hit from a financial reward register almost the same in the brain. That means access to your reward system costs the other person nothing. The question is whether you would hand anyone else that kind of access for free.

cards.title: The Pause After the Compliment Is Where the Ask Lives
cards.hook: Watch the three seconds after someone praises you. That pause is not accidental. They are waiting for the warmth to settle before they speak.
cards.truth:
The pause after praise is a timing move, not a gap in the conversation.
• Silence lets the good feeling grow before the ask breaks it.
• You feel pressure to fill the quiet — often by asking what they need.
• If they speak first, the ask arrives when you are most open to it.
cards.remember: The silence after a compliment is the setup for what comes next.
cards.theySee: A person who just said something warm, now sitting quietly with hands relaxed on the table, not moving.

signals.t: They hold eye contact through the pause — they are not done yet.
They do not turn away or pick up their phone after the compliment lands.
You fill the silence yourself with 'oh thanks, sure, what do you need?'
They shift slightly forward just before they finally speak.

steps.title: Receive the compliment and stop
steps.desc: Say 'thank you' and nothing else. Full stop. Do not explain, qualify, or deflect.

steps.title: Hold your ground in the silence
steps.desc: Do not fill the pause. Let it run. Whoever speaks next controls the next move.

steps.title: Let them name the ask out loud
steps.desc: When they do speak, pay attention to every word they use. That is the real agenda.

cards.counter:
If you feel the urge to fill silence after being praised, you are about to do their work for them.
• Notice: discomfort in the pause — the urge to say something, anything, to break it.
• Say: nothing. Let the silence run three more seconds.
• Do: let them make the ask in their own words, on the record.
cards.insight: Most people hate silence so much they volunteer the yes before they have been asked. The person running the setup knows this. They are not waiting out of politeness — they are waiting because you will fill the gap cheaper than they can.

cards.title: Generic Praise Creates a Debt You Cannot Name
cards.hook: "You are amazing" lands differently than "that report you filed saved us three hours." Vague praise puts you in debt you cannot locate or repay.
cards.truth:
Generic praise is harder to deflect because you do not know what you did to earn it.
• You cannot point to a specific act, so you cannot say 'that was a one-time thing.'
• You feel pressure to live up to a standard you do not understand and cannot control.
• This gives the other person room to move the bar whenever they want.
cards.remember: Vague praise puts you in debt you cannot name or repay.
cards.theySee: A friend looking you in the eyes and saying you are one of the most reliable people they know — before they have said what they need.

signals.t: The praise is about something you are, not something specific you did.
You say 'oh stop' because you are not sure what to do with praise you cannot verify.
They circle back to the same compliment later in the same conversation.
After the praise, you feel like you have to act a certain way or disappoint them.

steps.title: Ask what they mean
steps.desc: Say: 'What made you think of that?' Make them point to something specific you did.

steps.title: Do not absorb the label
steps.desc: Treat 'you are amazing' as their opinion, not a fact about you. It is their move, not your identity.

steps.title: Answer the ask on its own
steps.desc: When the request comes, evaluate it without the praise in the room. Would you do this for a stranger?

cards.counter:
Vague praise is designed to make you feel seen without giving you anything solid to push back on.
• Notice: compliments about who you ARE, not what you specifically DID.
• Say: 'What specifically did you have in mind?' Make them name the act.
• Do: if they cannot name the act back, the praise was not about the act.
cards.insight: The person who praises you in vague terms has more room to move than the one who names what you did. A specific compliment ends the conversation. A vague one is a credit line they plan to draw on later.

cards.title: Identity Praise Locks You In
cards.hook: "You are so good at this" sounds like a compliment. It is also a chain. Now you have to keep being good at it — or admit they were wrong about you.
cards.truth:
Praise about who you are, not what you did, turns your ego into a control switch.
• Your ego needs to stay consistent with the identity you have been handed.
• You will take on tasks — even bad ones — to protect the label.
• Refusing looks like admitting the praise was wrong, which almost nobody will do.
cards.remember: Accept the label, and you accept all the work attached to it.
cards.theySee: An employee nodding eagerly after their boss says 'You are the only person here who really gets the big picture.'

signals.t: The praise was about an adjective: smart, reliable, the best, a natural.
The compliment singles you out as special, not just as someone who did a good job once.
An assignment appears within hours or days of the identity praise.
They mention nobody else could do this — only you would understand.

steps.title: Notice the trait word
steps.desc: Listen for adjectives applied to you directly: smart, reliable, creative, best. Write them down when you hear them.

steps.title: Separate the trait from the task
steps.desc: Say to yourself: being [reliable] does not mean I have to do [this specific task]. Keep those two things apart.

steps.title: Accept the praise, answer the ask separately
steps.desc: Say: 'Thank you — walk me through what is involved.' Treat the compliment and the work as two different conversations.

cards.script: "I appreciate that — tell me more about what you would need."
cards.counter:
When someone praises your identity to get your behavior, refusing feels like denying who you are.
• Notice: trait praise followed quickly by a request only YOU can do.
• Say: 'I would want to know more about the scope before I take this on.'
• Do: evaluate the task on its own merits, not on whether it fits the label they gave you.
cards.insight: Children told they were smart were 20% more likely to cheat to stay smart. The same move runs in every office and every household. The harder question is: which labels have you already swallowed, and who put them there?

cards.title: The Size of the Compliment Matches the Size of the Ask
cards.hook: When someone praises you three times before getting to the point, they need something they already expect you to refuse.
cards.truth:
People scale their praise to the size of what they are about to request.
• A small ask gets a small compliment. A big ask gets an avalanche of them.
• The bigger the flattery, the more they expect resistance from you.
• They are loading up your goodwill because they know the ask is a stretch.
cards.remember: The more they praise you, the bigger the ask they are hiding.
cards.theySee: A coworker who has complimented your work twice before even sitting down, smiling a little too wide and a little too long.

signals.t: They have praised you more than once before naming what they actually want.
The praise is bigger or warmer than anything they have said to you before.
Nothing you did recently could explain this level of recognition.
Despite the warm words, they seem tense or like they planned what they were going to say.

steps.title: Count the compliments
steps.desc: Track how many times they have praised you before asking for anything. More than two in one conversation is a signal.

steps.title: Assume the ask is bigger than you expect
steps.desc: Tell yourself: this request will be something I would normally push back on. Prepare that answer before they speak.

steps.title: Ask for the details in writing
steps.desc: Once the ask is on the table, say: 'Can you send me the details?' Writing makes the request real and slows the social pressure.

cards.counter:
Over-the-top praise is a sign they have already calculated your likely answer and they do not like it.
• Notice: warmth that feels larger than the relationship warrants.
• Say: 'What is the situation?' Make them put the ask on the table.
• Do: calibrate your answer to the request, not to how good the praise made you feel.
cards.insight: The size of the flattery is their estimate of how hard a sell this will be. That estimate is information. The harder question is what they already know about the ask — that you do not know yet.

cards.title: Praise Is the Opening Move in a Trade
cards.hook: Praise puts something in your hands. Reciprocity makes you want to give something back. The person praising you knows this. You are already in a trade before the ask is named.
cards.truth:
Praise activates the same reciprocity wiring that responds to gifts and favors.
• You received something — praise — so you feel social pressure to return something.
• The something they want back is a yes, your time, or a favor.
• The wiring is automatic. You have to actively override it.
cards.remember: Praise is a gift they give so you will give something back.
cards.theySee: A colleague who just said something warm, now watching your face and waiting for you to respond.

signals.t: After the praise, you notice a pull to do something kind in return.
Saying no after being praised feels wrong, not just uncomfortable.
Their body language says they expect more than a thank-you — they expect a yes.
They give the compliment and then go quiet — leaving the trade hanging in the air.

steps.title: Name the move to yourself
steps.desc: Say internally: 'They just gave me something. I am feeling the pull to give back. That is reciprocity.'

steps.title: Return the compliment and stop
steps.desc: Say thank you in one clean line. Do not add anything that sounds like you are offering something.

steps.title: Evaluate the ask cold
steps.desc: Before agreeing, ask yourself: would I do this if no praise had come? If no, the praise changed your answer.

cards.script: "I appreciate that. What did you have in mind?"
cards.counter:
Praise-as-gift is the cleanest version of the setup because you feel the social debt without being told about it.
• Notice: the pull to give something back right after a compliment lands.
• Say: 'Let me hear what you need first.'
• Do: treat the praise and the request as two separate transactions.
cards.insight: The reciprocity wire does not care whether the praise was real or manufactured. It fires either way. The next question is what other social wires are running in the same conversation that you have not named yet.

cards.title: Accept the Praise, Answer the Ask Separately
cards.hook: You do not have to reject the praise to reject the ask. Treat them as two different conversations. One is about your work. The other is about their need.
cards.truth:
Most people bundle the praise and the request together — and you do not have to go along with that.
• Accepting praise does not mean accepting the obligation that follows it.
• Separating them puts you back in control of each decision on its own terms.
• You can be genuinely glad for the credit and still say no to what comes after.
cards.remember: A yes to the compliment is not a yes to the favor.
cards.theySee: A person who smiles and says thank you to the compliment, then pauses a full beat before saying anything about the request.

signals.t: They phrase the ask as a natural follow-on: 'Since you are so good at this, could you...'
Saying yes to the praise and no to the ask feels like a contradiction to you.
You feel like rejecting the ask somehow cancels the compliment they gave you.
The request comes within thirty seconds of the compliment, with no breathing room.

steps.title: Receive the compliment cleanly
steps.desc: Say 'thank you' and mean it. Do not qualify it, deflect it, or minimize it.

steps.title: Pause before addressing the ask
steps.desc: Wait at least three full seconds after the compliment before saying anything about what they want.

steps.title: Answer the ask on its own terms
steps.desc: Say: 'On the project — let me tell you where I am with my plate right now.' Treat it like a new, separate conversation.

cards.script: "Thank you for saying that. On the project — let me check what I have room for."
cards.counter:
If someone ties the praise and the ask together in one sentence, they are doing the bundling deliberately.
• Notice: phrases like 'since you are so great at this' used as a bridge to the request.
• Say: 'I hear both of those — let me answer them separately.'
• Do: confirm the compliment, then evaluate the ask as if no compliment had been given.
cards.insight: Separating praise from the ask sounds obvious. Doing it while the warmth is still there, in real time, takes daily practice most people have never done. The harder problem is what to say when they push back on the separation.

cards.title: Ask What They Need Before the Praise Finishes Landing
cards.hook: The fastest way to defuse the setup is to get the ask on the table early. Name it before they do. You lose the warmth — and gain the upper hand.
cards.truth:
The setup depends on you receiving the full praise before you know the cost.
• Asking early reverses the sequence — you see the ask before your guard is down.
• They are forced to name the request without the buildup doing its full work.
• It signals you know the pattern. Most people will immediately recalibrate.
cards.remember: Ask what they need before the praise finishes warming you up.
cards.theySee: A person who smiles politely but immediately says 'what is going on?' before the conversation gets any further.

signals.t: The compliment comes in the first two sentences, before any real topic is introduced.
Their tone is warmer than usual from the very first word of the conversation.
You can tell they came looking for you — they had a reason to find you specifically.
It feels like a prepared speech, not a passing comment they made in the moment.

steps.title: Cut the warmup short
steps.desc: After the first compliment, say: 'That is kind of you — what is the situation?' Do not wait for the full buildup.

steps.title: Get the ask in your hands early
steps.desc: Once you hear the request, evaluate it before the praise has had time to fully settle in.

steps.title: Answer the ask, not the praise
steps.desc: Respond directly to the request. Do not reference the compliment in your answer.

cards.script: "That is kind of you — what is the situation?"
cards.counter:
If cutting the warmup short makes someone uncomfortable, you just confirmed the warmup was intentional.
• Notice: surprise or resistance when you ask the question early.
• Say: nothing more — wait for the answer to 'what is going on?'
• Do: note whether they named the ask readily or kept steering back to praise.
cards.insight: Most people wait politely through the full buildup, which means the setup works every time they run it. Cutting it short is a small social disruption. The person who built the sequence did not plan for that.

cards.title: Pressure to Stay Praise-Worthy Is the Long Game
cards.hook: Once you accept a label — reliable, the best, indispensable — you are on the hook to keep earning it. The first praise was the setup. Every task after it is the extraction.
cards.truth:
The threat of losing a label drives more behavior than the original reward did.
• You work harder to avoid losing 'most reliable' than you ever did to earn it.
• This gives the person who named you ongoing access to your effort.
• The label does not need to be renewed — it runs on your own fear of losing it.
cards.remember: Keeping a label costs more than earning it did.
cards.theySee: An employee staying late on their own, not because anyone asked, but because they cannot afford to stop being the dependable one.

signals.t: Nobody asked — but you are doing extra work to stay consistent with what they said about you.
You are the last one there, not from a specific request but from fear of how it looks if you leave.
They have added more expectations since the original praise without giving any new credit for the extra work.
They keep referencing the original praise — 'as always' or 'that is why we count on you.'

steps.title: Audit the labels you carry
steps.desc: Write down three things people call you at work or home. For each one, list what tasks have come attached to that label.

steps.title: Test whether the label still serves you
steps.desc: Ask: does keeping this label cost me more than it gives me? If yes, you are being extracted from.

steps.title: Let one thing slip on purpose
steps.desc: Say no to one small task tied to a label this week. See whether the relationship survives. It usually does.

cards.script: "I am at capacity on that one — who else could take it?"
cards.counter:
When you feel fear of disappointing rather than motivation to do good work, the label is running you.
• Notice: anxiety about saying no, even when you have a clear reason.
• Say: 'I want to make sure I do this right — let me check my plate.'
• Do: evaluate the task on whether it is worth doing on its own, separate from the label.
cards.insight: The label gives whoever gave it to you a standing claim on your effort — and you enforce it yourself. The person who named you reliable does not even have to ask anymore. The harder question is who gets more out of the label: you or them.

cards.title: Real Praise Sounds Different From Setup Praise
cards.hook: Genuine praise names what you did and stops there. Setup praise names what you are and keeps going. One ends the conversation. The other opens it.
cards.truth:
Specific praise attached to a concrete act is the one kind that does not run a trade.
• It names the behavior: what you did, when, and what it changed for someone.
• It carries no obligation — there is nothing you are expected to return.
• It ends the conversation rather than opening one.
cards.remember: Real praise names the act. Setup praise names the person.
cards.theySee: A manager who looks you in the eye and says 'that call you handled on Thursday kept the client — I wanted you to know that' and then walks away.

signals.t: They named something you did, when you did it, and what it changed for someone else.
After the praise, they leave or change the subject — no ask comes after it.
The praise came in a moment when there was no obvious favor they needed from you.
You feel good but you do not feel watched or like you owe anything.

steps.title: Check whether an act was named
steps.desc: After someone praises you, ask: did they name something specific you did, or just describe what kind of person you are?

steps.title: Wait sixty seconds
steps.desc: After praise lands, wait a minute. If nothing comes after it, it may be real.

steps.title: Receive it and move on
steps.desc: If it passes both checks, say thank you and mean it. Do not look for a setup that is not there.

cards.counter:
Not all praise is a setup. Treating every compliment as a trap makes you paranoid and unpleasant to work with.
• Notice: specific act named, no ask following, nothing unusual about the timing.
• Say: 'Thank you.' Full stop.
• Do: use the same standard when you give praise — name the act, not the person.
cards.insight: Learning to detect setups can make you see them everywhere. The skill is telling the difference — not refusing all praise. The harder problem is that even real praise can be used as a setup later, after the relationship shifts.

cards.title: Name the Pattern Out Loud to Stop It Cold
cards.hook: Most setups dissolve the moment you name them. The person running it relied on you not seeing it. Say what you see, and the move is over.
cards.truth:
Naming the setup out loud is the highest-risk, highest-payoff counter available.
• It forces them to either confirm the setup or deny it on the record.
• Denial is fine — the behavior usually stops regardless.
• The move works because setups depend entirely on your silence.
cards.remember: Name the move out loud. Setups only work when you stay quiet.
cards.theySee: A person who heard the compliment, stayed calm, and said in plain words exactly what they noticed happening in the room.

signals.t: This is the third or fourth time the same praise-then-ask sequence has run with this person.
The ask is larger than anything they have asked before — and they built up to it longer than usual.
They are praising you and steering toward a decision in the same breath.
The praise is happening in front of other people who can see whether you agree or refuse.

steps.title: Wait until you are certain
steps.desc: Do not name it early. Let the ask land. Confirm the pattern is clear before you open your mouth.

steps.title: Name it calmly
steps.desc: Say what you observed in plain words, with no heat. Angry naming sounds defensive. Calm naming sounds dangerous.

steps.title: Wait for their response
steps.desc: After you name it, say nothing. Let them answer. Whatever they say tells you everything you need to know about what comes next.

cards.script: "I notice you usually say something nice about my work right before a big ask. What is the ask this time?"
cards.counter:
Naming a setup misfires if the praise was real and the ask was a coincidence — not a pattern.
• Notice: are you seeing a real pattern, or are you primed to find one after reading this dossier?
• Say: nothing until you are certain. One data point is not a pattern.
• Do: if you name it wrong, own the mistake cleanly — 'I misread that, tell me more.'
cards.insight: The person who names a manipulation out loud, without anger, is rare. Most people know they are being played and say nothing. Saying something changes the social dynamic in the room permanently — and what you do in the thirty seconds after determines whether that change works for you or against you.
